summary: Gives information on how to prepare RFCs and describes certain policies about their publication. It was the guide authors used for the format and process of the series. It replaced RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543, and was in turn replaced by RFC 7322.

eli5.summary: It is the style guide and rulebook for people writing RFCs. It was later replaced by a newer one.

subtitle: The 1997 rulebook for how to format an RFC and how the RFC Editor handles submissions.

tldr.problem: RFCs are read, searched and printed on a wide variety of equipment, and the RFC Editor needs submissions that follow one consistent style.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out the editorial policy, strict ASCII and PostScript format rules, the layout of the headers, the required sections, and how Updates and Obsoletes are used.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543, and was itself obsoleted by RFC 7322, so it is no longer the current guide.

facts.label: Status queries
facts.value: No more than once a week

today: RFC 2223 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 7322, which is now the place to look for RFC style guidance. It was itself published as the replacement for RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543, and was later updated by RFC 5741 and RFC 6949.

sections.title: Why RFCs Have a Strict Format
sections.content:
This memo gives information about preparing RFCs and about certain policies for publishing them. The RFC series covers a broad range of interests. Its core topics are the Internet and the TCP/IP protocol suite, but any topic related to computer communication may be acceptable at the discretion of the RFC Editor.

Anyone may submit a memo. A large source of memos is the IETF, where working groups evolve Internet Drafts until they feel the drafts are ready. The IESG reviews them and, if approved, sends them to the RFC Editor.

The format matters because online files are copied by interested people and printed or displayed on a wide variety of equipment. The primary RFC is always an ASCII text file. Secondary versions may be provided in PostScript, mainly to allow diagrams and drawings, but people also search RFCs with text tools such as emacs and grep and quote excerpts in e-mail, which is not yet practical with PostScript.
sections.eli5: Lots of people read RFCs on lots of different computers and printers. So everyone has to write them in the same plain style, like a class that all hands in work on the same kind of paper.

sections.title: Editorial Policy and Submission
sections.content:
Proposed RFCs are reviewed by the RFC Editor and possibly by other reviewers the Editor selects. The review may suggest improvements, may conclude that the document is not appropriate to publish as an RFC, or may add a statement about the ideas in it when they are relevant but inappropriate or unsafe. The RFC Editor may make minor changes to style, format and sometimes text, though more often the memo is returned to the author.

Documents that specify standards track protocols must be approved by the IESG before they are sent to the RFC Editor. The communication comes from the Secretary of the IESG and usually names the exact Internet Draft by file name. The RFC Editor assumes only that file is to be processed, so authors with small corrections send them separately, or as a diff, rather than sending a new version.

The ASCII version is the primary one. A PostScript version must match it, and the RFC Editor must decide that it is the same before it is published. Publication time varies. Authors may ask about status, but not more than once a week, and the two weeks before an IETF meeting are generally very busy.
sections.eli5: An editor reads your paper first and may ask you to fix things. You hand in the exact version that was approved, and you may ask how it is going, but only once a week.

sections.title: ASCII and PostScript Format Rules
sections.content:
Two formats are allowed: ASCII and PostScript. Authors must submit an editable online document, and should copy the style of recent RFCs. Most RFCs are processed with the unix nroff program using a simple set of requests from the ms macro package.

The ASCII rules are strict:

  • Each page is limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed on a line by itself.
  • Each line is limited to 72 characters followed by carriage return and line feed.
  • No overstriking or underlining, no right-margin padding, no hyphenation at the margin, and no footnotes.
  • Text is single spaced within a paragraph, with one blank line between paragraphs.

The height and width limits include headers, footers, page numbers and left indenting. Because page numbers change on reformatting, cross references by section number are easier to keep correct than references by page number.

The PostScript rules call for an 8 1/2 by 11 inch page with 1 inch margins and main text of no less than 10 points on 12 point line spacing. Three fonts are acceptable: Helvetica, Times Roman and Courier, plus their bold and italic versions. A list of PostScript commands, such as initgraphics and erasepage, should not be used.
sections.eli5: The rules say how many lines go on a page and how wide each line can be, so every page looks the same on any printer.

sections.title: Headers, Footers and Required Sections
sections.content:
The first page heading holds, on the left, Network Working Group, Request for Comments: nnnn, any Updates or Obsoletes line, the category and any FYI, BCP or STD numbers. On the right it holds the author's name (first initial and last name), the organization and the month and year. The title is centered below, and periods are not allowed in titles. The RFC Editor fills in the actual number at the last moment.

From page 2, the running header has the RFC number on the left, a possibly shortened title in the center and the date on the right. The running footer on all pages has the author's last name, the category and the page number as [Page N].

The category is one of Standards Track, Best Current Practice, Informational or Experimental, and the first page must carry a matching "Status of this Memo" paragraph plus the distribution statement. A copyright notice follows it. Every RFC should have an Introduction that explains its motivation, and it must have a Security Considerations section near the end, a References section in the series' own style, an Author's Address section at the very end, and a Full Copyright Statement on the last page. Standards track documents that use capitalized requirement words refer to BCP 14, RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Every RFC has the same label on top, the same footer on every page, and the same standard parts, like a school report with a cover, an intro and a list of sources.

sections.title: Updates, Obsoletes and Where RFCs Are Listed
sections.content:
An RFC can relate to an earlier one in two ways. A document that Obsoletes an earlier one replaces it and can be used alone, whether it has revised information or all the old information plus something new. A document that only Updates an earlier one supplements it, cannot stand alone and has limited usefulness independently. The terms Supercedes and Replaces are no longer used.

In lists of RFCs and in the RFC index, but not on the RFCs themselves, Obsoleted-by and Updated-by may be used to point from early documents to later ones.

RFC announcements go out on two mailing lists, IETF-Announce and RFC-DIST, and the memo advises not being on both. Several organizations keep RFC Index files, usually named rfc-index.txt, and copies from different sites may not be identical. The definitive statement on standards and their publication is the Internet Official Protocol Standards memo, STD 1.
sections.eli5: If a new RFC replaces an old one, it says "obsoletes". If it only adds a few pages to an old one, it says "updates".
